name: Ingain
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: As seguintes interpretações sobre o uso do acento agudo <´> podem ser levantadas: (i) indicação de tonicidade; (ii) distinção da qualidade vocálica; e (iii) uso assistemático dos diacríticos. [...] há nas anotações de VO um aspecto sistemático de ‘supressão de acento’ em termos derivados ou quando são o primeiro elemento em composições [...] Tais ocorrências parecem dar mais suporte para a interpretação (i), dado que possivelmente a palavra fonológica nesta língua apresente um padrão acentual oxítono (como também é o caso em Xokleng e Kaingang). [...] Dadas estas circunstâncias, as sílabas tônicas serão neste estudo interpretadas como tendo um padrão similar ao existente em Xokleng e Kaingang.
new_statements.translation: The following interpretations of the use of the acute accent <´> can be raised: (i) indication of stress; (ii) distinction of vowel quality; and (iii) unsystematic use of the diacritics. [...] in VO's [Vogt 1904] notes there is a systematic pattern of 'accent suppression' in derived words or when they are the first element of compounds [...] Such occurrences seem to give more support to interpretation (i), given that the phonological word in this language possibly has an oxytone [final-stress] accentual pattern (as is also the case in Xokleng and Kaingang). [...] Given these circumstances, the stressed syllables will in this study be interpreted as having a pattern similar to the one found in Xokleng and Kaingang.
new_statements.citation: Jolkesky, Marcelo Pinho de Valhery. 2010. Reconstrução fonológica e lexical do Proto-Jê Meridional. Dissertação de mestrado, Universidade Estadual de Campinas (IEL).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Ingain is taken to fall on the final syllable of the phonological word (oxytone), as in its sister languages Kaingang and Xokleng; this is an inference/assumption from legacy wordlist transcriptions (chiefly the loss of the acute on first members of compounds in Vogt 1904, e.g. kundá 'maize' vs kundagrón 'roasted maize'), not an observed description, and the author treats the collectors' acute accent itself as primarily a vowel-quality mark.
new_statements.exceptions: Author notes counter-indications: many mono- and polysyllables carry no accent at all, some words carry two acutes (e.g. <téktéknajá> 'run', <péingrahá> 'make fire'), and in several items the acute sits on what by Kaingang/Xokleng comparison should be an unstressed echo-vowel syllable (<loró> 'skin', <noró> 'sleep', <varý> 'far'); hence the diacritic is judged ambiguous and the final-stress pattern is adopted by analogy.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word, including compounds (stress on the last member: kundagrón, kambrá, kyprobán); evidence is isolated citation forms in 1893-1903 wordlists (Ambrosetti 1896, Vogt 1904). Vogt 1904:354 independently defines his acute as 'Betonungsakzent' (stress accent).
new_statements.identity_note: Ingain is extinct and attested only in 19th/early-20th-c. wordlists (Ambrosetti 1896: four lists from Tatinyupí/Alto Paraná informants; Vogt 1904: 'Ingain-Ivytorocái' lists Vo1/Vo3 from Marcelino Rivero and three Ivytorocái boys). Jolkesky 2010 analyses exactly this Ingain corpus (his sec. 4.5) and keeps Kimdá (Lista 1883/Patiño; Glottolog kimd1235) apart as unanalyzable; Nikulin 2020 treats Ingain and Kimdá as one language (= Glottolog subfamily inga1253 'Ingain-Kimda'). The statement quoted applies to inga1254 proper. Vogt 1904:354 states that in his own transcription the acute is a 'Betonungsakzent' (stress mark), so the Vo1 Ingain forms carry first-hand stress marks, but no placement rule is given there.

sources.citation: Jolkesky, Marcelo Pinho de Valhery. 2010. Reconstrução fonológica e lexical do Proto-Jê Meridional. Dissertação de mestrado, Universidade Estadual de Campinas (IEL).

sources.note: Sec. 4.5.1.2.1 'Acentuação' (pp. 131-134): the acute accent in the Ingain lists is ambiguous (stress vs vowel quality vs unsystematic); accent suppression on first elements of compounds in Vogt's list supports an oxytone phonological word 'como também é o caso em Xokleng e Kaingang'; tonic syllables are therefore interpreted as patterning like Xokleng/Kaingang (final stress). Elsewhere: Kaingang (p.83), Xokleng (p.117) and Proto-Southern-Jê (p.213f) all described as predictable final-syllable stress.

sources.citation: Vogt, P. Fr., S.V.D. 1904. Die Indianer des Obern Paraná. Mitteilungen der Anthropologischen Gesellschaft in Wien 34: 200-221, 353-377 (part II 'Die Indianer der Coroados-Gruppe', incl. '2. Die Indianer am Arroyo Ivytorocái' = Ingain and the comparative 'Wörterverzeichnisse der Coroados-Gruppe am Obern Paraná', pp. 359 ff., compiled with P. W. Schmidt).
sources.note: p. 354 transcription key: 'ě = ö, ˜ = Nasallaut, ´ = Betonungsakzent' (acute = stress accent); p. 360: his Ingain (Vo1) and Kaingang (Vo2) lists use 'die allgemein wissenschaftliche' Schreibweise. No statement of where stress falls; Ingain items carry mostly final acutes (kundá, nangrá, kendá, takrí, kypró...) and lose them as first members of compounds (observation made explicit by Jolkesky 2010:133).

sources.citation: Nikulin, Andrey. 2020. Proto-Macro-Jê: um estudo reconstrutivo. Tese de doutorado, Universidade de Brasília.
sources.note: Nothing on Ingain stress. Sec. 1.1.1.4 (p.16): Ingain material is 'extremamente limitado... pequenas listas de palavras transcritas de forma não uniformizada'; fn. 73 (p.87): no reliable synchronic phonological analysis of Ingain exists, Jolkesky 2010's rests on many ad hoc premises.
